title: Absolute-stability region: which h*lambda are stable?
summary: The picture that tells you, for a given time-stepping method, which values of the scaled eigenvalue h lambda keep the numerical solution bounded. The stability region is a shaded area of the complex plane; the problem's eigenvalues are plotted on top of it.

media.alt: Complex plane with the shaded RK4 stability region and a dashed Euler circle; five orange stable points inside and one rose cross outside on the negative real axis.
media.caption: Reference render of class F5.2 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Which h*lambda are stable?
read_the_figure.axes: x: Re(h lambda). y: Im(h lambda). Equal aspect, so the circle is round. The origin and the axes are drawn as thin lines.
look_at: Which side of the contour |R| = 1 is shaded (stable), and where does the region cut the negative real axis?
Is every point h times lambda of the problem inside the region? Name any that is outside.
How does the second method's contour compare in width along the real axis and along the imaginary axis?
Does the region include a piece of the imaginary axis (so pure oscillations are damped or neutral)?
as_drawn: The shaded region and solid contour belong to RK4. The dashed circle of radius 1 centred at -1 belongs to explicit Euler.

Six values of h lambda are plotted for h = 0.5 and lambda = -1, -2 plus or minus 2i, -0.5 plus or minus 3i, -6. Five are inside the RK4 region (orange discs); the one at -3 (lambda = -6) is outside (rose cross).
The RK4 region reaches about -2.79 on the real axis and about 2.9 up the imaginary direction, so it is wider than Euler's, whose circle reaches -2.
The legend is placed over the upper left of the plot, in the empty part of the plane.
read_the_figure.proves: If every scaled eigenvalue h lambda of a linear problem lies inside the region, the numerical solution of that problem does not grow. It says nothing about accuracy, and for nonlinear problems it is only a guide through the linearisation.
if_wrong: A scaled eigenvalue just outside the contour: reduce h, or switch to a method whose region contains it. Stability returns for an h small enough to pull the point inside.
The region drawn for the wrong polynomial or the wrong sign: check that R(0) = 1 and that the contour passes through the origin region you expect.
Eigenvalues plotted without multiplying by h: the points do not belong in this plane.
must_check: |R| = 1 contour: this is the boundary between growth and decay, and everything else on the plot is read against it.
eigenvalues of the problem overlaid: the region on its own is a property of the method; the overlaid h lambda points connect it to your problem.

terms.meaning: The scalar problem y' = lambda y used to study stability. Eigenvalues of a linear system play the role of lambda.
One step of a method applied to the test equation gives y_{n+1} = R(z) y_n. R depends only on the method.
The product of step size and eigenvalue, the single complex number that decides stability.
The set of z for which |R(z)| is at most 1: the numerical solution of the test equation stays bounded.
y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(y_n). Its stability function is 1 + z.
The classical fourth-order Runge-Kutta method. On the test equation it reproduces the Taylor polynomial of e^z to degree 4.

remember: y_{n+1} = R(h lambda) y_n, so the solution decays when |R| < 1.
Explicit Euler: stable inside the unit disc centred at -1; real limit h lambda > -2.
RK4: real limit h lambda > -2.785 (found from R(x) = 1).
Stiff problems have large |lambda|, so an explicit method needs a tiny h to pull h lambda inside.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position is the complex number z = h lambda: real part across, imaginary part up. The shaded area is the set of stable z. The solid teal line is the RK4 boundary and the dashed blue circle is explicit Euler's. Orange discs and the rose cross are the problem's scaled eigenvalues; shape as well as colour separates stable from unstable.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: In plain words: whether a method blows up on a linear problem is decided by one number per eigenvalue, the step size times the eigenvalue. Plotting that number on the complex plane next to the method's safe area turns a calculation into a look: a point inside is safe, outside is not. Because eigenvalues can be complex (oscillation), the plane is needed, not just a line.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Only linear constant-coefficient behaviour is shown: for nonlinear problems the eigenvalues move along the trajectory, so one snapshot is not enough (see F5.4 for the step trace). Being inside the region guarantees boundedness, not a correct answer, and a point very near the boundary may decay so slowly that the solution is wrong long before it blows up. The axes must have equal scale, otherwise the shape of the region is distorted.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: The eigenvalue scatter against the unit circle (F5.3) shows the same fact in the plane of R(z) instead of z. For a fixed problem, a plot of the largest stable step against the stiffest eigenvalue (F5.4) is more practical. For implicit methods the region contains the whole left half-plane, which is easier to state in words.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add the stable region of a second-order method and of implicit Euler on the same axes, colour the eigenvalues of a particular problem by the largest stable step they allow, and mark the real-axis limit of each region with a tick.

steps.title: One step on the test equation
steps.note: Stable means |R(z)| is at most 1, so that R(z)^n does not grow.

steps.title: The two stability functions
steps.note: Euler's region is |1 + z| at most 1, a disc. RK4's is the lump in the figure.

steps.title: Real-axis limits
steps.note: Solve numerically for RK4. The maximum stable step for an eigenvalue lambda < 0 is these limits divided by |lambda|.

worked.title: Is lambda = -6 stable at h = 0.5 with RK4?
worked.problem: Using the figure: (1) Which of the six plotted points are unstable and why? (2) For lambda = -6 and RK4, how small must h be? (3) Does Euler's region contain the points that RK4's region contains?

solution.text: (1) The cross at z = -3 is outside the shaded region. Evaluate RK4's stability function there.
So the solution grows by a factor 1.375 each step, which matches the cross. The other five points have |R| of 0.37 to 0.75 and are inside.
(2) The real-axis limit is -2.785, so h lambda must be at least -2.785.
(3) No. For example z = -0.25 + 1.5i has |1 + z| = 1.68, outside the dashed circle but inside the shaded RK4 region. The RK4 region contains the Euler disc, plus more.

worked.answer: The cross is unstable because |R(-3)| = 1.375. With RK4 the step must be below about 0.46 for lambda = -6 (Euler would need less than 0.33). RK4's region is larger than Euler's.

analyze.q: Estimate from the figure the largest h for which all six eigenvalues are stable with RK4. Which eigenvalue sets the limit?
analyze.hint: Scale the z points back along the ray from the origin.

analyze.q: An oscillator has eigenvalues plus and minus i omega. Does explicit Euler's region touch the imaginary axis away from the origin? What happens to a pure oscillation?
analyze.hint: Check |1 + i y| for y not zero.

analyze.q: Why does a stiff problem push you toward an implicit method?
analyze.hint: Compare the sizes of the two regions in the left half-plane.

evaluate.q: All of your plotted points are inside the region. Is the simulation therefore accurate?
evaluate.hint: What question does the region answer, and what does it not?

create: Plot the stability region of RK4 yourself with a contour of |R(z)| at the level 1 on a 500 by 500 grid, then add the Euler circle.
Choose a problem with two eigenvalues, one slow and one fast, and show on the plot the step at which the fast one leaves the region.

checks.q: Why does the plot use the complex plane and not just a line?
checks.answer: Eigenvalues can be complex when the system oscillates; the stability of the method depends on both the real and imaginary part of h times lambda.

checks.q: Euler is used with h = 0.5 on lambda = -5. Is it stable?
checks.answer: z = -2.5, |1 + z| = 1.5 > 1, so no. The limit for lambda = -5 is h < 0.4.

checks.q: A point sits just inside the region boundary. Why might the solution still be poor?
checks.hint: How fast does |R|^n decay when |R| is near 1?
checks.answer: Near the boundary |R| is close to 1, so errors decay very slowly and the numerical solution can be inaccurate for many steps even though it is bounded; stability is not accuracy.
